..
Issued at 223 AM CDT Tue Sep 1 2026

The 00Z analysis shows a strong anticyclone centered over the 
southern into the central Plains with a compact low over the 
Canadian Prairies and the jet running along the international 
border. A trough is digging into the Pacific Northwest while 
Tropical Storm Edouard sits just off the Louisiana coast. WV imagery 
suggests dry and subsident air over the region beneath the ridge, 
with monsoon moisture streaming across the Desert Southwest into the 
Rockies. At the surface the weak quasi-stationary boundary that held 
northern Kansas a few degrees cooler Monday has lifted into 
Nebraska, leaving the entire area in the warmer air to the south. 
H85 temperatures in the middle 20s C supported yet another day with 
temperatures around 100 degrees at many area locations.

The forecast question this period continues to center on whether 
heat headlines will be needed and when, and it revolves around 
dewpoint uncertainty. Ensemble high temperatures remain tightly 
clustered in the upper 90s, near 100 across north central Kansas, 
with spread of only a few degrees through Saturday. Ensemble 
dewpoints are not as clear. The mean sits near 60 today, dips 
Wednesday in association with some of the deepest mixing of the 
week, then climbs into the middle 60s Thursday and Friday in 
association with southerly return flow and holds through the 
weekend. The member spread for Thursday and Friday runs from the 
upper 50s to the upper 60s, and that spread will ultimately factor 
into the headline decision making. Low 60s dewpoints yield heat 
indices near 100 and no advisory issue, but still hot and dry. 
Middle 60s, the current ensemble mean, push heat indices to 103 to 
105. Upper 60s bring the 105 to 107 range. NBM heat index 
probabilities follow the same trend, with values above 100 likely 
Thursday and Friday, while 105 remains unlikely for most of the area 
but still possible across north central Kansas late week. Near-
record warm overnight lows add to the overall concern with little 
cooling to start the day. Lows in the middle and upper 70s puts 
Topeka and Concordia on record warm minimum watch through Thursday 
morning. No headline is currently needed for today as confidence in 
the temperature forecast is high. With the depth of mixing and thus 
the distribution of moisture through the boundary layer dewpoints 
today should hold in the low to mid 60s.

The ridge still holds through the Labor Day holiday weekend.
Ensemble mean mid level heights over Topeka dip slightly Thursday as 
a low amplitude northern stream disturbance passes well to the north 
of the area, then the ridge re-amplifies and builds directly over 
the central Plains Saturday through Tuesday with tight overall 
member agreement. H85 temperatures hold in the middle 20s C through 
the same period with no meaningful downward trend, and WPC cluster 
analysis keeps the ridge axis over Kansas in every cluster through 
Monday. That continues to argue against the NBM cooling trend for 
the weekend, which reflects widening spread in the tails rather than 
a shift in the mean, and highs were held in the upper 90s through 
Sunday and middle 90s on Labor Day. Rain chances remain minimal 
through Friday barring an unforeseeable mesoscale change to the 
going forecast pattern. Slight chances for precipitation return 
Saturday onward as the western flank of the ridge works east, 
possibly allowing smaller scale mesoscale complex activity to push 
into the area, but predictability is low at this time.

The overall weather pattern may finally change by mid to late next 
week as a more amplified Pacific trough swings through the northern 
Plains in the Thursday time frame. Ensemble mid level heights hold 
through Wednesday and then fall sharply, hinting at a frontal system 
working into the region. Meanwhile, H85 temperatures in the LREF 
drop several degrees C as well, which appears to be the first real 
cooling signal in the current guidance. Cluster analysis splits 
sooner, in the Tuesday time frame, between holding the ridge and 
flattening it. Either way, the signal is that a change in airmass 
may finally be on the way.
